packages.name: com.landawn.abacus.da.aws
packages.summary: Root package of the AWS data-access integrations.

packages.name: com.landawn.abacus.da.aws.dynamodb
packages.summary: Provides synchronous and `com.landawn.abacus.util.ContinuableFuture`-based access to Amazon DynamoDB through AWS SDK for Java 1.x.

types.name: AsyncDynamoDBExecutor
types.javadoc_summary: Asynchronous wrapper around `DynamoDBExecutor` providing task-based operations against the AWS SDK v1 (`com.amazonaws.services.dynamodbv2`) DynamoDB client.

methods.name: sync
methods.signature: public DynamoDBExecutor sync()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the underlying synchronous DynamoDBExecutor.
methods.returns: the underlying synchronous `DynamoDBExecutor` instance
contract: This method provides access to the wrapped synchronous executor, allowing you to perform blocking operations when needed.
This is useful when you need to mix synchronous and asynchronous operations in your application.

methods.name: getItem
methods.signature: public ContinuableFuture<Map<String, Object>> getItem(final String tableName, final Map<String, AttributeValue> key) throws IllegalStateException, RejectedExecutionException

params.name: tableName
params.javadoc: the name of the DynamoDB table to retrieve the item from, must not be `null`

params.name: key
params.javadoc: the primary key of the item to retrieve, must include all key attributes, must not be `null`

throws.condition: if the backing AsyncExecutor has been shut down before task submission
if the backing executor refuses the submitted task because its queue is full or it has shut down

methods.javadoc_summary: Asynchronously retrieves an item from the specified DynamoDB table.
methods.returns: a `ContinuableFuture` containing the item as a Map of attribute names to values, or `null` if the item doesn't exist
contract: If the item doesn't exist, the future will complete with `null`.

Usage Examples: The returned future completes exceptionally if the SDK cannot send the getItem request, DynamoDB rejects its table, key, conditions, or service limits, or a returned item cannot be converted to the requested Java representation.

methods.name: getItem
methods.signature: public ContinuableFuture<Map<String, Object>> getItem(final String tableName, final Map<String, AttributeValue> key, final Boolean consistentRead) throws IllegalStateException, RejectedExecutionException

params.name: tableName
params.javadoc: the name of the DynamoDB table to retrieve the item from, must not be `null`

params.name: key
params.javadoc: the primary key of the item to retrieve, must include all key attributes, must not be `null`

params.name: consistentRead
params.javadoc: `Boolean.TRUE` for a strongly consistent read; `Boolean.FALSE` or `null` for an eventually consistent read

throws.condition: if the backing AsyncExecutor has been shut down before task submission
if the backing executor refuses the submitted task because its queue is full or it has shut down

methods.javadoc_summary: Asynchronously retrieves an item from the specified DynamoDB table with configurable read consistency.
methods.returns: a `ContinuableFuture` whose payload is a `Map<String, Object>` of attribute names to values, or `null` if the item doesn't exist
contract: Read Consistency Trade-offs: Eventually Consistent (false/null): Lower latency, better throughput, half the read capacity cost Strongly Consistent (true): Guaranteed latest data, higher latency, full read capacity consumption Usage Examples: The returned future completes exceptionally if the SDK cannot send the getItem request, DynamoDB rejects its table, key, conditions, or service limits, or a returned item cannot be converted to the requested Java representation.

methods.signature: public ContinuableFuture<Map<String, Object>> getItem(final GetItemRequest getItemRequest) throws IllegalStateException, RejectedExecutionException

params.name: getItemRequest
params.javadoc: the complete GetItemRequest with all parameters configured, must not be `null`

throws.condition: if the backing AsyncExecutor has been shut down before task submission
if the backing executor refuses the submitted task because its queue is full or it has shut down

methods.javadoc_summary: Asynchronously retrieves an item using a complete GetItemRequest for maximum control.
methods.returns: a ContinuableFuture containing the item as a Map of attribute names to values, or `null` if the item doesn't exist
contract: Advanced Features Available: Projection expressions to retrieve only specific attributes Expression attribute names for reserved word handling Consistent read configuration per request Return consumed capacity for monitoring read capacity usage Usage Examples: The returned future completes exceptionally if the SDK cannot send the getItem request, DynamoDB rejects its table, key, conditions, or service limits, or a returned item cannot be converted to the requested Java representation.

methods.name: getItem
methods.signature: public <T> ContinuableFuture<T> getItem(final String tableName, final Map<String, AttributeValue> key, final Class<T> targetClass) throws IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, RejectedExecutionException

params.name: tableName
params.javadoc: the name of the DynamoDB table to retrieve the item from, must not be `null`

params.name: key
params.javadoc: the primary key of the item to retrieve, must include all key attributes, must not be `null`

params.name: targetClass
params.javadoc: the class to convert the item to, must not be `null`; the supported types are those of `DynamoDBExecutor#getItem(String, Map, Class)`: an entity class, which needs a no-args constructor, a builder, or a constructor taking all its properties in declaration order (as a record's canonical constructor does), a `Map` class, an object-array or collection class, or a single-value type for an item with exactly one attribute

throws.condition: if `targetClass` is null
if the backing AsyncExecutor has been shut down before task submission
if the backing executor refuses the submitted task because its queue is full or it has shut down

methods.javadoc_summary: Asynchronously retrieves an item from the specified DynamoDB table and converts it to the target type.
methods.returns: a `ContinuableFuture` containing the item converted to type T; if the item doesn't exist, the default value of `targetClass`: `null` for entity, `Map`, collection, array, and most scalar types, the primitive default (e.g. `0` or `false`) for a primitive, an empty `Optional`, `OptionalInt` (and the like) or `Nullable` for those wrapper types, and a `Holder` of `null` for `com.landawn.abacus.util.Holder`
contract: Type Conversion Features: Automatic mapping from DynamoDB AttributeValues to Java types Support for primitives, wrappers, String, and numeric types Handling of complex types like Lists, Sets, and Maps Null-safe conversion for missing or null attributes Custom POJO mapping using reflection Usage Examples: The returned future completes exceptionally if the SDK cannot send the getItem request, DynamoDB rejects its table, key, conditions, or service limits, or a returned item cannot be converted to the requested Java representation.

methods.name: batchGetItem
methods.signature: public ContinuableFuture<Map<String, List<Map<String, Object>>>> batchGetItem(final Map<String, KeysAndAttributes> requestItems) throws IllegalStateException, RejectedExecutionException

params.name: requestItems
params.javadoc: a map where keys are table names and values are `KeysAndAttributes` objects specifying the items to retrieve from each table, must not be `null`

throws.condition: if the backing AsyncExecutor has been shut down before task submission
if the backing executor refuses the submitted task because its queue is full or it has shut down

methods.javadoc_summary: Asynchronously performs a batch get operation to retrieve multiple items from multiple tables.
methods.returns: a `ContinuableFuture` containing a map of table names to lists of retrieved items, where each item is represented as a Map of attribute names to values
contract: If any requested items are not found, they will simply be omitted from the results.

Unprocessed keys are silently dropped: when DynamoDB leaves some keys unprocessed (throttling or response-size limits), this method does not auto-retry them; because it returns only the responses map — as does every `batchGetItem` overload on this executor — any unprocessed keys are lost.

Usage Examples: The returned future completes exceptionally if the SDK cannot send the batchGetItem request, DynamoDB rejects its table, key, conditions, or service limits, or a returned item cannot be converted to the requested Java representation.

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts a DynamoDB item (map of AttributeValues) into an instance of the specified entity class.
methods.returns: the converted entity instance, or `null` if `item` is `null`
contract: For each attribute in `item` the converter: looks up the matching property on `targetClass` (using the property name, then any `@Column`/`@Table` column-to-property map), and writes the converted value if found; if the attribute name contains a `'.'` (dot) and no top-level property matches, treats it as a nested-property path and assigns into the nested bean, converting the value as for the last property of the path named directly.

The dependency's path setter creates a missing intermediate bean through its no-args constructor and assigns into an existing one in place, so a path through a nested record (or another bean without a no-args constructor) fails the item (`IllegalArgumentException` for a missing intermediate bean, `ClassCastException` when an earlier attribute already set it); read such a nested bean from an `M` attribute instead.

A path through a collection property is left whole to the dependency's path setter, which writes into the first element of the collection, or into a new bean it adds when the collection is missing or empty; in a builder-built target it reads the first property of the path from the builder and fails the item with `ClassCastException`; silently ignores attributes that match neither a property nor a dotted path, and attributes of read-only properties, which cannot be assigned.

In a mutable bean a getter without a setter is a property only in an `@Entity` class or a subclass of one, where `#toItem(Object)` writes its value: it is such a read-only property when no field of the same name backs it (a computed value) or it is marked `@AccessFieldByMethod`, and is otherwise assigned through that field.

A binary value for a typed collection or object array becomes its single element when the elements are binary or untyped and supplies its byte values when they are other scalars, also in directly mapped beans; a binary value for a typed map, a pair or other parameterized type, or a collection of containers or beans is rejected.
An effective date format takes precedence over the number format, so an unsupported date format on a numeric wrapper is rejected even when a number format is present.
Recursive generic beans retain these rules even when a property becomes a numeric wrapper only after several recurrences.
The complete formatted value must match; trailing content is rejected.
A bean with none of these (for example only a constructor taking some of its properties) fails with `UnsupportedOperationException` when an item is present.
examples:
Map<String, AttributeValue> item = dynamoDBClient.getItem(tableName, key).getItem();
User user = DynamoDBExecutor.toEntity(item, User.class);

contract: It automatically handles pagination when no exclusive start key is supplied.

methods.name: close

methods.javadoc_summary: Closes this async executor and releases the resources held by the underlying client.
contract: After calling this method, no further operations should be performed on this executor — they will fail because the underlying client is closed (with the default Netty HTTP client, the returned future fails with an `SdkClientException` wrapped in a `CompletionException`; the `stream` and `scan` futures still complete normally, and consuming their stream throws the `SdkClientException`).
Note on shared clients: if the `DynamoDbAsyncClient` passed to the constructor is also used elsewhere, calling `close()` here will close it for those callers too.

Resource Management: Closes all HTTP connections in the connection pool Shuts down internal async thread pools Releases NIO channels and buffers Any in-flight requests may fail with an SDK shutdown error Best Practices: Always call `close()` when finished with the executor Call `close()` from a finally block for guaranteed cleanup Avoid calling `close()` while operations are still pending For graceful shutdown, wait for outstanding `CompletableFuture`s to complete first Usage Examples:

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts a DynamoDB item Map to a Java entity of the specified class.
methods.returns: an instance of `targetClass` populated from `item`, or `null` if `item` is `null`
contract: Such a path is assigned through the dependency's path setter, which creates a missing intermediate bean through its no-args constructor and assigns into an existing one in place: a path through a nested record or another bean without a no-args constructor fails the item (`IllegalArgumentException` when the intermediate value is missing, `ClassCastException` when an earlier attribute already set it); read such a nested bean from an `M` attribute instead.

A path through a collection property is left whole to the dependency's path setter, which writes into the first element of the collection, or into a new bean it adds when the collection is missing or empty; in a builder-based `targetClass` it reads the first property of the path from the builder and fails the item with `ClassCastException`.

In a mutable bean a getter without a setter is a property only in an `@Entity`-annotated class or a subclass of one, where `#toItem(Object)` writes its value: it is such a read-only property when no field of the same name backs it (a computed value) or it is marked `@AccessFieldByMethod`, and is otherwise assigned through that field.

A binary value for a typed collection or object array becomes its single element when the elements are binary or untyped and supplies its byte values when they are other scalars, also in directly mapped beans; a binary value for a typed map, a pair or other parameterized type, or a collection of containers or beans is rejected.
An effective date format takes precedence over the number format, so an unsupported date format on a numeric wrapper is rejected even when a number format is present.
Recursive generic beans retain these rules even when a property becomes a numeric wrapper only after several recurrences.
The complete formatted value must match; trailing content is rejected.

types.name: CassandraExecutor
types.javadoc_summary: Primary Cassandra database executor providing high-level CQL operations and result mapping.

constructors.signature: public CassandraExecutor(final CqlSession session) throws IllegalArgumentException
constructors.javadoc_summary: Creates a new CassandraExecutor with the specified Cassandra session.

params.name: session
params.javadoc: the Cassandra session to use for database operations

throws.condition: if `session` is `null`

examples:
CqlSession session = CqlSession.builder()
    .addContactPoint(new InetSocketAddress("127.0.0.1", 9042))
    .withLocalDatacenter("datacenter1")
    .withKeyspace("my_keyspace")
    .build();
CassandraExecutor executor = new CassandraExecutor(session); // ready to use; null session throws IllegalArgumentException

constructors.signature: public CassandraExecutor(final CqlSession session, final StatementSettings settings) throws IllegalArgumentException
constructors.javadoc_summary: Creates a new CassandraExecutor with the specified session and statement settings.

params.name: session
params.javadoc: the Cassandra session to use for database operations

params.name: settings
params.javadoc: default statement settings for statements this executor prepares/binds/batches, or null for defaults

throws.condition: if `session` is `null`

examples:
StatementSettings settings = StatementSettings.builder()
    .consistency(ConsistencyLevel.QUORUM)
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(30))
    .fetchSize(1000)
    .build();
CassandraExecutor executor = new CassandraExecutor(session, settings); // settings may be null (driver defaults are used)

params.name: row
params.javadoc: the Cassandra Row containing the data

params.javadoc: the target entity class with getter/setter methods (must not be `null`)

throws.condition: if `row` or `entityClass` is `null`, or `entityClass` is not a bean class (it has no property getter/setter methods or public fields, or it is a `Map` type, including an `@Entity`-annotated `Map` subclass; use `#toMap(Row, IntFunction)` for a map)

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts a single Cassandra Row to an entity object.
methods.returns: a new instance of the entity class populated with row data
contract: The method handles: Direct mapping: Column names matching property names exactly Name variants: a column name also matches a property case-insensitively or in its snake_case form (e.g., `first_name` to `firstName`), as the bean metadata resolves it, or by the property's declared `@Column` name (see `QueryUtil#columnToPropNameMap(Class)`); no executor naming policy is involved, since this method is static Nested properties: Dot-notation property paths (e.g., `"address.city"`) when no direct property is found; the value is converted for the path's last property as a top-level column value is, and a path that does not resolve, or whose last property is read-only, is ignored.

A missing intermediate bean is created through its no-argument constructor and assigned first, and the value is written into the instance its owner then holds (the created one when the getter returns a new copy on every read), so a setter that stores a copy of its argument keeps the value Type conversion: Automatic conversion between compatible types (see the class documentation for the `timestamp`, `date`, `inet` and `blob` rules; a `blob` read into a `String` property is the base64 text of its bytes, one read into a property declared as a collection of an element type is that collection of the blob converted to the element type, one read into an `Optional`, `Nullable` or `Holder` property is that wrapper of the blob converted to its element type (an `Optional<ByteBuffer>` the buffer, a `Nullable<byte[]>` its bytes), and one read into a number, date/time, `UUID` or other property without a blob form fails the row), for top-level and nested properties alike.

A collection or map column read into a property declared as a parameterized collection or map (for example `List<byte[]>` or `Map<String, String>`) or as an object array has each element, key and value converted by the same rules for the declared element type, nested containers included (a `list<timestamp>` into a `List<LocalDateTime>`, a `set<inet>` into a `Set<String>`); the driver's collection is set unchanged when every element already has its declared type, and otherwise a new one of the declared kind holding the converted elements in the driver's order.

    String.class, "SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = ?", unknownId); // returns Nullable.empty() when no row matches

// Row matched but column is NULL -> present-but-null (NOT empty)

    String.class, "SELECT nickname FROM users WHERE id = ?", userId); // Nullable.of(null) when the row exists but column is NULL

types.name: UDTCodec
types.javadoc_summary: Abstract base class for creating custom User Defined Type (UDT) codecs.

methods.name: create
methods.signature: public static <T> UDTCodec<T> create(final UserDefinedType userType, final Class<T> javaClazz) throws IllegalArgumentException

params.name: userType
params.javadoc: the Cassandra User Defined Type to map

params.name: javaClazz
params.javadoc: the Java class to map the UDT to

throws.condition: if `javaClazz` is `null`

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a new instance of a UDTCodec for the specified User Defined Type (UDT) and Java class.
methods.returns: a new instance of `UDTCodec` for the specified UDT and Java class
contract: When `javaClazz` is a `Collection` type, values are mapped positionally in UDT field order.

When `javaClazz` is a `Map` type, a value is written from the entries keyed by the exact (internal) field names, a missing field being written as `null` and other entries ignored, and decodes to a map keyed by the field names.

When it is a bean class, each field is bound to the property of that name (matched case-insensitively or in its snake_case form, as `CassandraExecutor#toEntity(Row, Class)` matches a column) or to the property declaring it as its `@Column` name.
A field without a matching property is written as `null` and ignored when decoding; a read-only (for example getter-only) property is written from its getter but ignored when decoding.

An entity property that holds a bean value of this codec (or a collection of them) must be annotated with `@Column` for the entity operations to write and read it: a bean-typed property without it is a sub-entity, which an entity `insert` or `update` and a query selecting all properties leave out without an error (see Entity-to-CQL mapping in `CassandraExecutorBase`).
If no registered codec accepts a `Date` or `Calendar` value, it is converted to `LocalTime` the same way ordinary parameter binding converts it.
Dates use the JVM default zone captured when Abacus's `com.landawn.abacus.type.AbstractTemporalType` is initialized; calendars use their own zone.
The `java.time` date-time types are not accepted when writing a TIME field unless a registered codec accepts them.

If no registered codec accepts another value, it is converted to an `Instant` as a value bound to a `timestamp` column is: a `LocalDateTime` or `LocalDate` in the JVM default zone (a `LocalDate` as the start of that day), a `ZonedDateTime` or `OffsetDateTime` as the instant it denotes, a `Date` (including `java.sql.Timestamp`) or `Calendar` as its instant, a `Long` as epoch milliseconds, and ISO-8601 instant text; a value that conversion rejects fails with the driver's `CodecNotFoundException`.
Usage Examples: The returned codec rejects unsupported Java types and collections with more elements than UDT fields when encoding or decoding a non-null value.
examples:
UserDefinedType userType = session.getMetadata()
    .getKeyspace("my_keyspace")
    .flatMap(ks -> ks.getUserDefinedType("my_udt"))
    .orElseThrow(() -> new IllegalArgumentException("UDT not found"));

UDTCodec<MyClass> codec = UDTCodec.create(userType, MyClass.class); // returns a codec marshaling MyClass to/from the UDT

types.name: ParsedCql
types.javadoc_summary: Immutable parsed CQL text and parameter metadata, with caching through `#parse(String)`.

methods.name: parse
methods.signature: public static ParsedCql parse(final String cql) throws IllegalArgumentException

params.name: cql
params.javadoc: the non-null CQL text; the untrimmed string is used as the cache key when eligible

throws.condition: if `cql` is null; if a recognized data operation contains an empty named placeholder, mixed parameter styles, or a MyBatis placeholder missing its closing brace; or if brackets, or a `#` that does not open a MyBatis marker, require masking but fewer than three unused mask characters are available

methods.javadoc_summary: Parses a CQL statement, reusing a cached result when available.
methods.returns: an immutable parsed result, newly created or retrieved from the cache
contract: Callers must not rely on reference identity.
examples:
ParsedCql parsed = ParsedCql.parse("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = :userId;");
parsed.parameterizedCql();       // "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?"
parsed.parameterCount();         // 1
parsed.namedParameters().get(0); // "userId"

ParsedCql.parse(null);                                    // throws IllegalArgumentException
ParsedCql.parse("SELECT * FROM u WHERE a = ? AND b = :x"); // throws: mixed parameter styles
ParsedCql.parse("SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = #{}");         // throws: empty parameter name

methods.name: originalCql
methods.signature: public String originalCql()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the original CQL statement (with leading and trailing whitespace trimmed).
methods.returns: the trimmed original CQL statement string
contract: This is useful for logging, debugging, or when you need to preserve the original query format.
examples:
ParsedCql.parse("   SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = ?   ").originalCql(); // returns "SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = ?" (trimmed)
ParsedCql.parse("SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = :userId").originalCql(); // returns "SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = :userId" (placeholders kept)
ParsedCql.parse("SELECT id FROM u WHERE id = ?;").originalCql();     // returns "SELECT id FROM u WHERE id = ?;" (trailing ';' kept)

methods.name: parameterizedCql
methods.signature: public String parameterizedCql()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the normalized CQL text with recognized named placeholders replaced by `?`.
methods.returns: the normalized CQL text; empty if the input normalizes to an empty statement
contract: # AND c =?` keeps its text and has two parameters (Cassandra rejects the `#` when the statement is prepared).

Inside braces, a native named marker (`:name`) is recognized only when it follows a map/UDT field separator (`{street::street}`, `{street::street}`), follows an arithmetic operator (`+`, `-`, `*`, `/` or `%`; for example {f: 1 +:x}, {'a': -:x} or the second marker of {f::x -:y}), or sits directly inside a `[...]` or `(...)` nested in the braces (for example the tuple in `{loc: (:lat,:lon)}`).

methods.name: namedParameters
methods.signature: public ImmutableMap<Integer, String> namedParameters()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns a mapping of parameter positions to their original names.
methods.returns: an immutable map from zero-based parameter position to name, without `:` or `#{...}` delimiters; empty if no named placeholders were recognized

methods.name: parameterCount
methods.signature: public int parameterCount()
methods.javadoc_summary: Returns the number of recognized parameter occurrences in the CQL statement.
methods.returns: the number of recognized placeholders, always non-negative
contract: For recognized data operations, this count represents the number of parameter placeholders that need to be bound when executing the statement.
examples:
ParsedCql.parse("SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = ? AND status = ?").parameterCount();         // returns 2 (positional)
ParsedCql.parse("SELECT * FROM u WHERE id = :id AND status = :status").parameterCount(); // returns 2 (named)
ParsedCql.parse("SELECT * FROM u").parameterCount();                                     // returns 0 (no parameters)
ParsedCql.parse("CREATE TABLE t (id INT PRIMARY KEY)").parameterCount();                 // returns 0 (DDL: no parameter scanning)

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts a single Cassandra Row to an entity object.
methods.returns: an instance of the entity class populated with row data
contract: The method handles: Direct mapping: Column names matching property names exactly Name variants: a column name also matches a property case-insensitively or in its snake_case form (e.g., `first_name` to `firstName`), or by the property's declared `@Column` name (see `QueryUtil#columnToPropNameMap(Class)`); no executor naming policy is involved, since this method is static Nested properties: Dot-notation property paths (e.g., `"address.city"`) when no direct property is found; the value is converted for the path's last property as a top-level column value is, and a path that does not resolve, or whose last property is read-only, is ignored.

A missing intermediate bean is created through its no-args constructor and assigned first, and the value is then written into the instance its owner holds (so a setter that stores a copy of the bean keeps the value; the created one when the getter returns a new copy on every read) Null values: a `NULL` column sets the property to the default value of its type: `null` for a wrapper or other reference type, the primitive default for a primitive property (for example, `0` for an `int`), and an empty value for an `Optional`-like property Type conversion: a column value is converted to the property type (see the class documentation for the `date`, `timestamp`, `inet` and `blob` rules; a `blob` read into a `String` property is the base64 text of its bytes, one read into a collection property of another element type is its only element converted to that type, one read into an `Optional`, `Nullable` or `Holder` property is that wrapper of the blob converted to its element type (an `Optional<ByteBuffer>` the buffer, a `Nullable<byte[]>` its bytes), and one read into a number, date/time, `UUID` or other property without a blob form fails the row), for top-level and nested properties alike.

A collection or map column read into a property declared as a parameterized collection or map (for example `List<byte[]>` or `Map<String, String>`) or as an object array has each element, key and value converted by the same rules for the declared element type, nested containers included (a `list<timestamp>` into a `List<LocalDateTime>`, a `set<inet>` into a `Set<String>`, a `list<time>` into a `List<LocalTime>`); the driver's collection is set unchanged when every element already has its declared type, and otherwise a new one of the declared kind holding the converted elements in the driver's order.

    "SELECT count(*) FROM users WHERE status = ?", "active"); // present Nullable holding the count

    BigDecimal.class, "SELECT max(salary) FROM employees WHERE department = ?", "engineering"); // present Nullable (value may be null if no aggregate)

    String.class, "SELECT email FROM users WHERE id = ?", unknownId); // returns Nullable.empty() when no row matches

// Row matched but column is NULL -> present-but-null (NOT empty)

    String.class, "SELECT nickname FROM users WHERE id = ?", userId); // Nullable.of(null) when the row exists but column is NULL

executor.queryForSingleValue(int.class, "SELECT age FROM users WHERE id = ?", userId);     // Nullable.of(0)

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a ready-to-use UDT codec for the given user type and Java class.
methods.returns: a new UDT codec instance
contract: When the driver's codec registry is accessible reflectively, a registered codec accepting the value takes precedence, including a `Date` codec accepting a `java.sql.Time` or `java.sql.Timestamp`; its serializer failures propagate unchanged.
If no codec accepts a supported temporal value, the value's local time is encoded as nanoseconds since midnight.

An `java.time.Instant` uses the current JVM default zone; a `Date` uses the default zone captured when Abacus's `com.landawn.abacus.type.AbstractTemporalType` is initialized; a `Calendar` uses its own zone.
If reflective access to the driver's codec registry is unavailable, TIME fields use exact-runtime-class codec lookup.

Lookup and serialization then share one setter call: a `CodecNotFoundException` identifying CQL `time` and the value's exact runtime Java type triggers the built-in temporal conversion when that conversion supports the value, even if a registered codec threw the exception from its serializer.

A `CodecNotFoundException` identifying the exact runtime Java type and a supported `blob` mapping triggers the fallback even if a registered codec throws that exact exception from its serializer; other serializer failures propagate unchanged.

contract: Columns whose names contain a period are written via `BeanInfo#setPropValue(..., true)` so dotted paths can populate nested beans even when no top-level property matches; a nested bean the path has to create needs a no-argument constructor (a nested record fails the read with `IllegalArgumentException`; read it from a `STRUCT` column instead), and is assigned before the value is written into the instance its owner then holds, so a setter that copies the bean keeps it.

A direct column that matches a read-only property (one with no setter or permitted field write: a getter-only property, or a field restricted by `@AccessFieldByMethod` without a setter) is ignored, whatever its `@JsonXmlField` direction (an explicit `DESERIALIZE_ONLY` cannot make it writable); a dotted column is ignored when its terminal property is read-only.

methods.returns: a Stream containing all query results converted to the target type; later page-fetch and row-conversion failures are raised during stream traversal
examples:
// Advanced query with custom job configuration
QueryJobConfiguration config = QueryJobConfiguration.newBuilder(
    "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE status = 'active'")
    .setUseLegacySql(false)
    .setPriority(QueryJobConfiguration.Priority.INTERACTIVE)
    .setMaximumBytesBilled(10000000L)
    .setLabels(Map.of("environment", "production"))
    .build();

Stream<Customer> stream = executor.stream(Customer.class, config);   // query completed; row conversion is deferred
long count = stream.count();                                         // returns the number of rows produced by the job

// Query with caching disabled
QueryJobConfiguration noCacheConfig = QueryJobConfiguration.newBuilder(
    "SELECT * FROM realtime_data")
    .setUseQueryCache(false)
    .build();

executor.stream(Map.class, noCacheConfig)
    .forEach(System.out::println);

methods.javadoc_summary: Creates a new AnyAppend instance by copying an existing HBase Append operation.
methods.returns: a new AnyAppend instance backed by a fresh Append copied from `appendToCopy`
contract: Attributes (including the TTL, cluster ids, ACL, cell visibility and the return-results flag) and the priority are copied as well, but the Durability is not: HBase's copy constructor leaves it at `Durability.USE_DEFAULT`, so re-apply setDurability on the copy when the source used a non-default level.

Append existingAppend = new Append(Bytes.toBytes("user123"));

                         Bytes.toBytes("login;"));

assert append.val() != existingAppend;                 // true: the wrapped Append is a distinct copy
append.addColumn("logs", "activity", "logout;");       // returns the same AnyAppend; does not mutate existingAppend

Performance Benefits: Dramatically reduces I/O when filtering on specific columns Reduces network traffic by not loading unnecessary column family data Most beneficial with `SingleColumnValueFilter` and `filterIfMissing=true` Important Consistency Considerations: Enabling on-demand loading can lead to inconsistent results in concurrent environments: Phantom Rows: Concurrent updates to multiple column families may result in rows with mixed old/new data that never actually existed as a consistent snapshot.

contract: This variant uses the Put's default timestamp at the time of the call — the one it was constructed with or last set via `#setTimestamp(long)` (or `HConstants.LATEST_TIMESTAMP` when none was supplied, in which case the region server stamps the cell when the mutation is applied).
Every call appends a cell to this client-side Put, even when the family and qualifier repeat.
examples:
AnyPut put = AnyPut.of("user123")
    .addColumn("info", "name", "John Doe")             // String value; returns the same AnyPut
    .addColumn("info", "age", 30)                      // Integer value
    .addColumn("stats", "balance", 1000.50)            // Double value
    .addColumn("meta", "created", new Date());         // Date value
boolean stored = put.has("info", "name", "John Doe");  // true

// A null value is permitted and stored as an empty value.
AnyPut p2 = AnyPut.of("row").addColumn("info", "q", (Object) null);
int size = p2.size();   // 1 (the cell is still added)

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts a single HBase `Result` into an instance of `targetType`.
methods.returns: the converted entity, or the type's default value if the result is empty
contract: For JavaBean target classes this performs full object-relational mapping: the row-key cell (if a row-key setter is registered or discovered via `@Id`) populates the row-key property, and each subsequent cell is matched to a bean property using the entity's column-family/qualifier mapping.

Only that write path decides: a `@JsonXmlField(direction = SERIALIZE_ONLY)` property that has a setter is still written on read (as in DynamoDB item mapping), and a read-only property is still skipped when its field declares `DESERIALIZE_ONLY`.

The one exception is a read-only mutable nested bean that is flattened into its own column family (the family is the nested bean property, the qualifiers are its properties) and held by a field: its cells are written into the instance that field already holds, which needs no setter; when that field holds `null` the whole family is skipped and the rest of the row is still read (a read-only immutable nested bean cannot be filled in place, so its family is always skipped).

Otherwise a flattened mutable nested bean that the property of a mutable entity already holds is filled in place (the instance the property returns at the row's first cell of that bean; if the property returns another instance after the last cell, as a getter that copies or builds a new view on each call does, the filled one is assigned to it through its setter), and any other flattened nested bean is created for the row and assigned to its property once, after the last cell of the row, so a setter or builder method that copies its argument receives it complete.

Such a nested bean may be immutable (a record, or a bean built through its constructor or builder): it is built from its cells, and a nested property without a cell gets its default value or, only when the owning entity is mutable, the value it has in the instance the property already holds (the nested value that the builder or constructor of an immutable entity starts with is not consulted).

A property without a cell, such as one that was `null` or an empty value wrapper (empty `Optional`/`Nullable`/`OptionalInt` and the like, a `Holder` of `null`) when `AnyPut#create(Object)` wrote the row, is not assigned and keeps the value a new instance has.

A cell that several properties can write (under the same or different naming policies) is ambiguous: the value it holds belongs to whichever of them was written to it, so it is routed as in earlier versions, to the family's first nested bean when that bean knows the qualifier, else to another nested bean of the family that knows it (in no specified order), and only one of the writers can read it back.

For single-value target types the `Result` must contain exactly one cell, whose value is decoded into `T` — via `Type#valueOf(String)` for text-decoded types, while `byte[]` and `ByteBuffer` targets receive a copy of the raw cell bytes; a result with more cells triggers `IllegalArgumentException`.

contract: Use this overload when you need a specific `Date` implementation such as `java.sql.Date`, `java.sql.Timestamp`, or a custom `Date` subclass.
present semantics: `Nullable.empty()` is returned only when no document matches the filter.

examples:

        Filters.eq("recordId", "R001"), Timestamp.class); // present (value may be null) if a doc matched; Nullable.empty() if none

        Filters.eq("userId", "u1"), java.sql.Date.class); // converted to java.sql.Date; Nullable.empty() if no doc matched

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns a stream of distinct values for the specified field.

methods.javadoc_summary: Converts a MongoDB query result to a strongly-typed List.
methods.returns: a List containing all results converted to the specified type (empty list if no results). Null rows retain their positions, including when every result is null. When a result is a non-`Document` `Map` and a different concrete map type is requested, its entries are copied directly rather than being interpreted as bean properties; for an entity `rowType` such a row is mapped like a `Document` (including the `_id` handling of `#toEntity(Document, Class)`). Scalar results whose Java type differs from a scalar `rowType` (e.g. `Integer` values requested as `Long`) are converted individually; BSON dates requested as `LocalDate`, `LocalDateTime` or `LocalTime` are read in UTC, as the driver's codecs write those types.
contract: A map target creates every row's map with one factory: when the first non-null row is a Document, `IntFunctions#ofMap(Class)` with the row's size, including registered map creators, as for a Document result; otherwise `N.newMap(Class)`, as for other rows.

When the rows are documents (maps), an object-array or `Collection` `rowType` is a single-value target like a scalar one: each row's sole non-`_id` field (or its `_id`) is converted to it, so a projected BSON array field reads into a `String[]` or `List`, and a row with several non-`_id` fields is rejected with `IllegalArgumentException`.
Other rows must already be instances of such a `rowType`.

methods.javadoc_summary: Extracts selected properties from a list of objects into a Dataset with typed rows.
methods.returns: a Dataset containing the extracted properties as typed rows
contract: The method handles different input types intelligently: Map objects: Extracts the selected keys as a Dataset row; a Map target preserves Map structure, while a bean target converts each Map row (a `Document` or any other `Map`) to the bean Document objects: Converts to target type using the framework's type conversion system Other objects: A bean row is converted to a map for a Map target, or copied to a bean target of another class; other rows (positional `Object[]` or collection rows, scalars) are passed to the Dataset as-is and read against `selectPropNames` (or, when it is null or empty, against the column names taken from the first row), without per-row conversion to the target type Rows may mix these shapes.

With a Map target and a Map first row, bean rows are converted to maps and positional rows and scalars are left as-is; but when `selectPropNames` is null or empty the column names are collected from the keys of every row, so each row must then be a Map or a bean (a null row or any other row is rejected).

A BSON value type with bean-like accessors (a `Binary`, `Code` or `Symbol`, or a `BsonValue` such as `BsonBinary`) is a scalar here, although `Beans.isBeanClass` is true for it: like any other scalar row it fills the single column rather than being read as a bean of its own properties, and is rejected with `IllegalArgumentException` unless the Dataset has exactly one column (so also when it is the first row and `selectPropNames` is null or empty).
With a Map target, a Map first row and no `selectPropNames` it is always rejected, even when every map has a single key, since the column names are then collected from every row.

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns a `Mono` that, on subscription, queries for the given property of the first matching document, converted to the specified type.
methods.returns: a `Mono` that emits the converted field value on subscription, or completes empty when no document matches or the field is missing/null (for a primitive `valueType`, a missing/null field on a matched document emits the primitive default instead)
contract: The value is converted to `valueType` via binary-aware scalar conversion: binary payloads can be read as byte arrays or readable `java.nio.ByteBuffer` values; a BSON date requested as `java.time.LocalDate`, `java.time.LocalDateTime` or `java.time.LocalTime` is read in UTC; text enclosed in `[...]` requested as an array type whose elements accept text (such as `String[]` or `Object[]`) is parsed as the JSON array text earlier versions stored for an array (`"[a, b]"` becomes `{"a", "b"}` and `"[]"` an empty array; text that does not parse becomes the single element); an embedded document requested as a bean class is read as the embedded document of a bean property is read (the elements of a `List<Long>` property become `Long`s, a `LocalDate` property is read in UTC, a `String` or `ObjectId` id property takes the document's own `id` field, if any, over its `_id`), and an array of embedded documents requested as a bean array likewise element by element; other values use `com.landawn.abacus.util.N#convert(Object, Class)`.

present semantics: the returned `Mono` completes empty when no document matches the filter, or when a matching document's named field is absent or BSON null (or holds a value that converts to `null`, such as empty text requested as a number or date).

Subscribers cannot distinguish "no document matched" from "document matched but value is null" purely from the reactive signal — use the blocking sync API (`com.landawn.abacus.da.mongodb.MongoCollectionExecutor`) when that distinction is required.
Usage Examples: After subscription, the returned publisher signals a `MongoException` if the MongoDB read command fails.

Document decoding or result conversion failures are also signalled through the publisher, for example an `IllegalArgumentException` when the selected value cannot be converted to `valueType`, or the failure of constructing or populating a result bean.

throws.condition: if `fieldName` is null, empty, or contains an empty path segment (such as `"a..b"`)

methods.javadoc_summary: Returns distinct values of the specified field across the whole collection, each surfaced on an entity of the mapper's row type `T`.
methods.returns: a cold `Flux` that, on subscription, emits each distinct value of the field surfaced on an entity of type `T`, then completes; completes empty when the collection has no documents (documents that lack the field produce a single entity whose field value is `null`, except for a single-value `T`, which skips that `null` value)
contract: Each distinct value is surfaced under `fieldName` on an entity of the mapped type, and is only readable if the entity declares a matching property.

Internally this runs a `$group`/`$project` aggregation pipeline (the same approach as `#groupBy(String)`), so scalar field values decode cleanly into `T` — unlike the driver's native `distinct(field, T.class)`, which throws `BsonInvalidOperationException` when `T` is a POJO and the field is scalar.

When `T` itself is a single-value type (such as `String`, or a BSON value class such as `Binary` or `Code`), the `$project` stage is omitted and each distinct value is emitted directly, converted to `T`; for such a `T` the `null` value shared by documents that lack the field is not emitted, because Reactive Streams forbids `null` elements.
Usage Examples: After subscription, the returned publisher signals a `MongoException` if the MongoDB aggregate command fails.

methods.javadoc_summary: Opens a new `Session` directly via the underlying `SessionFactory`.
methods.returns: a fresh, unpooled OGM `Session`
contract: The OGM `Session` does not expose a `close()` method; `Session#clear()` releases the session's mapping context (the accumulated identity map of loaded entities) when the session is kept, except Neo4j-OGM's cache of graph IDs by primary-index value, so prefer short-lived sessions.

params.name: action
params.javadoc: the callback invoked with the pooled session; must not be `null`

throws.condition: if `action` is `null`
if `action` throws while using the borrowed session

methods.javadoc_summary: Borrows a pooled `Session`, hands it to `action`, and returns it to the pool when `action` completes (whether normally or exceptionally).
contract: Use this for multi-statement work that needs to share a single session (for example, when opening an explicit transaction via `Session#beginTransaction()` so that several saves commit atomically).

The server sees no lock cycle (the blocked caller is the holder's own thread), so its deadlock detection does not end the wait: it lasts until a configured lock-acquisition or transaction timeout ends it, and indefinitely when none is configured (Neo4j's default).

params.name: action
params.javadoc: the function invoked with the pooled session; must not be `null`

throws.condition: if `action` is `null`
if `action` throws while using the borrowed session

methods.javadoc_summary: Borrows a pooled `Session`, applies `action` to it, returns the result, and releases the session back to the pool when `action` completes (whether normally or exceptionally).
methods.returns: the value produced by `action`
contract: Important: `action` must not return or otherwise retain the `Session` itself because it is cleared (see `Session#clear()`) and returned to the pool when this method completes.
Entity objects may be returned, but they are detached from that cleared session and subsequent persistence work must use another executor operation or session.

methods.javadoc_summary: Loads a single mapped entity by its OGM identifier, populating related entities to the given depth.
methods.returns: the loaded entity, or `null` if no node with that ID exists
contract: `depth == 0` loads only the node's scalar properties; `depth == 1` loads it together with immediate relationships; larger depths recurse further; `-1` loads the entire connected sub-graph reachable from this node and should be used with care on large graphs.
examples:
Person personOnly = executor.load(Person.class, 123L, 0);   // properties only
Person withCompany = executor.load(Person.class, 123L, 1);  // immediate relationships
Person fullGraph = executor.load(Person.class, 123L, -1);   // full reachable sub-graph

methods.signature: public void delete(final Object object) throws IllegalArgumentException, RuntimeException

params.name: object
params.javadoc: a mapped entity, an array of mapped entities, or an `Iterable` of mapped entities to delete; must not be `null`. A `null` element of an array or `Iterable` fails with a `NullPointerException` before anything is deleted

throws.condition: if `object` is `null`; also thrown by Neo4j-OGM, before anything is deleted, if `object` (or one of its elements) is not an instance of a mapped entity class
if OGM cannot resolve the objects to delete, the database cannot be reached, or Neo4j rejects the delete query

methods.javadoc_summary: Deletes one or more OGM-managed entities from Neo4j.
contract: The entity must carry a populated graph ID (i.e.

When the cleared pooled session cannot resolve the graph ID — for every entity of a class without a native graph-ID field (primary index only), and for an entity whose native graph-ID field is `null` but whose class also has a primary index — OGM first reloads the entity by its primary-index value (and logs a warning) before deleting it.

The deletes of an array or `Iterable` are not atomic: Neo4j-OGM deletes each entity in a transaction of its own, so when one of them fails, the entities before it stay deleted and those after it are not attempted.

Deleting an entity of a class without a native graph-ID field and then saving a new entity with the same primary-index value works across executor calls, but not inside one such session: Neo4j-OGM keeps the deleted node's graph ID for that value, so the session sends the save as an update of the deleted node, which writes nothing (or, if Neo4j has meanwhile reused that graph ID for another node, overwrites that node).

methods.signature: public <T> Optional<T> findOnly(final Class<T> targetClass, final String cypher, final Map<String, ?> parameters) throws IllegalArgumentException, RuntimeException

params.name: targetClass
params.javadoc: the target class — either a mapped OGM entity class or a basic value type (e.g. `Long.class` for an aggregate result); pass the wrapper class, not a primitive class such as `long.class`, with which every non-`null` result fails (and, for a numeric primitive class, a `null` value too, because it is read as zero)

params.name: cypher
params.javadoc: the Cypher query string with `$name` parameter placeholders; must not be `null` or empty

params.name: parameters
params.javadoc: named parameters bound by the OGM session; may be empty but must not be `null`

throws.condition: if `targetClass`, `cypher`, or `parameters` is `null`

if `cypher` is empty or `targetClass` is a void type (Neo4j-OGM rejects these with a plain `RuntimeException`); if the database cannot be reached or Neo4j rejects the query; if the query produces more than one result (counted as described above); or if the result cannot be mapped to `targetClass` (Neo4j-OGM throws a `MappingException`, also for a result of a primitive `targetClass` as described above, because the value it maps is boxed)

methods.javadoc_summary: Executes a Cypher query and returns its single result mapped to `targetClass`, wrapped in an `Optional`.
methods.returns: an `Optional` describing the single mapped result, or an empty `Optional` if there is no result (no rows or, for an entity class, no entity of that class in the result) or the single value is `null` (for example `RETURN null`)
contract: The query must produce zero or one result; if it produces more, the underlying OGM session raises a `RuntimeException`.
Add a `LIMIT 1` clause or a uniqueness constraint to the Cypher when the query could otherwise produce several results.

methods.javadoc_summary: Executes a Cypher query and maps its result to instances of `targetClass`.
methods.returns: a `Stream` over the already-fetched results mapped to `targetClass` as described above; it does not retain the borrowed session
contract: `targetClass` is typically an OGM-mapped entity class for queries that return whole nodes, but may also be a basic value type when the `RETURN` clause produces a single scalar per row.
The two are mapped differently: For a basic value type, every row must have exactly one column, and the stream holds one converted value per row.

methods.name: count
methods.signature: public long count(final Class<?> targetClass, final Iterable<Filter> filters) throws IllegalArgumentException, RuntimeException

params.name: targetClass
params.javadoc: the OGM-mapped class whose entities are counted

params.name: filters
params.javadoc: OGM `Filter`s whose `org.neo4j.ogm.cypher.BooleanOperator`s define how each filter is joined to the preceding one; pass an empty iterable to count all entities of `targetClass`. The filters of a `Filters` object or of any other iterable are copied as described above. Unlike the `Filters` overloads of `loadAll`, a `null` iterable is not accepted here

throws.condition: if `targetClass` or `filters` is `null`

if `targetClass` is not a mapped entity class (Neo4j-OGM rejects it with a plain `RuntimeException`, whereas `#count(Class)` returns `0` for it), if a filter after the first has no `org.neo4j.ogm.cypher.BooleanOperator`, if OGM cannot map the filters, the database cannot be reached, or Neo4j rejects the count query

methods.javadoc_summary: Counts the number of mapped entities of the specified type that match the given filter expression.
methods.returns: the number of entities of `targetClass` that satisfy the supplied filter expression
contract: Original filter objects are passed on when an iterable contains a `null` element (Neo4j-OGM then throws a `NullPointerException`), an instance of a `Filter` subclass, or a filter whose nested path holds an instance of a `Filter.NestedPathSegment` subclass: Neo4j-OGM then resolves its filters in place, and two filters of a plain list on the same property share one parameter, the last value wins and the count is silently wrong.

All filter objects are passed on without copying (with a warning logged once) if the Neo4j-OGM `Filter` and `Filter.NestedPathSegment` classes on the classpath do not declare exactly the fields of Neo4j-OGM 5.0.7 through 5.0.11, or if the filter's private comparison function, which the copy reads reflectively, cannot be accessed (see "Filter Arguments" in the class documentation).

An iterable other than a `Collection` or `Filters` is consumed once into a list before copying: if a filter cannot be copied, that list preserves every original filter, including those already inspected.
